This is just an error in terminology. The US government works as a triumvirate of powers. Executive, Legislative, and Judicial. President, Congress, and the courts (including the Supreme Court).

A Monarchy has one ruler. The term Monarchy does not imply a hereditary post, length of post, or even how the post is chosen. Even if the US presidency was transformed into a hereditary position (which sounds like part of your fear) this would not make it a Monarchy. It would simply be a hereditary presidency. There are still the two other branches of the government to work with.

There have even been countries with elected monarchies. The monarch position would be chosen for a period and a new monarch would be elected. The Monarch part of the term mean that the monarch is the sole ruler of the country. So again, that would not fit for calling the US a monarchy even if the two main nominees are Bush and Clinton.

The three branches work together and adversarially. Congress can't make new laws without the President. The President can't invent a new law without it coming from Congress. (Yes. There are exceptions to both of these. But they are a minor aspect of the larger government process.) Congress and the President can't make new laws that are contrary to the Constitution without the courts having the ability to nullify them. Congress can't appoint the President, the President can't put people in Congress and nobody can fire the Supreme Court. (Again... Exceptions are minor. Don't get hung up on details and miss the big picture.)

In order to qualify as a Monarchy, the country would have to disband Congress and the court system leaving only one branch of government. Then the president would be a monarch (regardless of how the president is selected).
